questions.stem: Which minerals leaching from fields drive eutrophication?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Limestone calcium is not the fertiliser driver here.
Eroded iron is unrelated to fertiliser leaching.
Road salt is a different pollutant entirely.

questions.stem: What happens first after nitrates enter a lake?

options.explanation: Decomposers boom after the plant die-off.

options.text: Aquatic plants and algae overgrow at the water surface
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Fish deaths come last, after oxygen collapses.
Temperature is not the first event.

questions.stem: Why do plants below the surface die during eutrophication?

options.explanation: Nitrates feed plants; shade is what kills them.
Fish grazing is not the mechanism.

options.text: The surface overgrowth cuts the light reaching them
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They run out of carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is not the limiting factor being blocked.

questions.stem: How do decomposers lower dissolved oxygen?

options.explanation: Respiration uses oxygen; it does not emit a poison.
Gill clogging is not the documented route.
Water volume is unchanged; oxygen is consumed.

options.text: Their respiration consumes the oxygen dissolved in the water
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: What is the final stage of eutrophication?

options.text: Oxygen falls so low that many aquatic organisms die
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The lake becomes saltier than the sea
options.explanation: Salinity is not the endpoint described.
The boom collapses once light and oxygen fail.
No rock forms; the sequence ends in oxygen depletion.

questions.stem: State what leaching means in the context of fertilisers.
questions.modelAnswer: Leaching is the washing of soluble minerals, such as nitrates from fertiliser, out of soil into nearby water bodies.

questions.stem: Name the process that follows fertiliser leaching into lakes.
questions.modelAnswer: Eutrophication is the process that follows when fertiliser minerals are leached into lakes and streams.

questions.stem: Explain why decomposer numbers rise during eutrophication.
questions.modelAnswer: Decomposer numbers rise because the shaded aquatic plants die and leave abundant dead material for bacteria and fungi to feed on.

questions.stem: A farmer sprays fertiliser before heavy rain. Predict the lake downstream.
questions.modelAnswer: Rain leaches the nitrates into the lake, triggering algal overgrowth, plant death, a decomposer boom and falling oxygen, so fish and other aquatic organisms die.

questions.stem: How does sewage commonly reach rivers?

options.explanation: Roots cannot carry sewage into rivers.

options.text: When sewers overflow or heavy rain washes agricultural waste off fields
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Pipes carry treated water to taps, not sewage to rivers.
Evaporation does not transport sewage.

questions.stem: Which organisms multiply first when sewage enters a stream?

options.explanation: Fish larvae decline in polluted water.
Denitrifiers act on nitrates in soil, not sewage waste.

options.text: Aerobic bacteria that feed on the biological waste
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Algae bloom on nitrates in eutrophication, not on sewage waste directly.

questions.stem: What happens to dissolved oxygen after a sewage spill?

options.text: It rises with the extra waste
options.explanation: Waste feeds bacteria whose respiration consumes oxygen.
Bacterial respiration changes it measurably.
No such conversion happens.

options.text: It falls because the growing bacteria respire heavily
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which aquatic organisms survive a severe sewage pollution event?

options.text: Only species that tolerate low oxygen concentrations
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Oxygen-sensitive species die first.
Size does not grant oxygen tolerance.
Producers are not the survivors highlighted here.

questions.stem: Why does sewage pollution raise a second, invisible danger?

options.explanation: Oxygen never becomes toxic; pathogens are the hidden hazard.

options.text: Because pathogenic bacteria increase alongside the pollution
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Radioactivity plays no part here.
Fish do not turn venomous from sewage.

questions.stem: State the effect of sewage on aerobic bacteria in waterways.
questions.modelAnswer: Sewage provides biological waste, so aerobic bacteria feeding on it increase in number.

questions.stem: State the effect of sewage pollution on the biodiversity of an aquatic ecosystem.
questions.modelAnswer: Biodiversity decreases because oxygen-sensitive organisms die and only low-oxygen survivors remain.

questions.stem: Explain why sewage and fertiliser leaching produce similar oxygen crashes.
questions.modelAnswer: Both events feed large microbial populations whose respiration consumes dissolved oxygen, so both drive oxygen down until sensitive aquatic organisms die.

questions.stem: A town reports both an overflow and a fish kill downstream. Order the events.
questions.modelAnswer: The overflow released sewage, aerobic bacteria multiplied on the waste, respiration cut dissolved oxygen, and the fish died from oxygen shortage.
